1:
Henry reads the passage as a legal instrument, the Magna Charta of the new kingdom of nature, the former charter having been forfeited and seized; and adds that though the earth granted is a wilderness rather than a paradise, it is better than we deserve, and blessed be God it is not hell. Ellicott sets it beside the first charter: the blessing on the second father of mankind is exactly parallel to that given to the first, with two changes, that the animals are now given for food and that human life is newly guarded, the evident object being to prevent such a disruption of the race as followed Cain's murder of Abel. Gill limits the blessing to temporal things, since though some of them had spiritual ones, not all did, and particularly not Ham. Calvin infers from the length and repetition of the encouragement how greatly Noah had been dejected by fear, and notes that God sanctioned anew the law of marriage, since his blessing, though it extends in some way even to illicit connections, makes that an impure fruitfulness.

On the fear and dread three of them reach for the same rhetorical device. Henry asks what keeps wolves out of our towns and lions out of our streets, and confines them to the wilderness, but this fear. Calvin asks whence it arises that serpents spare us, and how tigers and lions and bears do not devour everything human, and answers that they are withheld by this subjection as by a barrier, providence being a secret bridle on their violence. Clarke turns it on a domestic animal and makes it an indictment: did the horse know his own strength, and the weakness of the wretch who unmercifully rides, drives, whips and goads him, would he not with one stroke of his hoof destroy his tyrant possessor? Gill adds a homelier explanation of the dominion's ready recovery: the creatures had lived with Noah in the ark so long.

Whether flesh was first permitted here is the chapter's oldest quarrel, and Calvin stands alone. Clarke says there is no positive evidence that animal food was used before the flood, Noah having the first grant of the kind; Wesley says man had hitherto been confined to the products of the earth, and that God now enlarged the grant and allowed flesh, which perhaps man never thought of till then; Ellicott records simply that the animals are now given for food. Keil takes a middle course: the words do not affirm that man then first began to eat animal food, but only that God then first authorised what he had probably been doing already against his will. Calvin denies the inference outright: God bestows nothing new but restores what had been taken away, since men had already sacrificed and killed wild beasts for hides and tents, and he sees no obligation that should have prevented their eating flesh; yet he adds that the point is of little consequence and affirms nothing about it.

Why the grant was enlarged just then Clarke and Wesley explain physiologically. Clarke argues that it would not have been made had no extraordinary alteration taken place in the vegetable world, rendering its productions less nutritive, and in the constitution of man, so that a grosser diet became necessary; the contracted lives of those after the flood are his evidence. Wesley suspects the flood had washed away much of the virtue of the earth, and rehearses the seven precepts the Jewish doctors held binding on all nations, against idols, blasphemy, murder, uncleanness and theft, and requiring justice. Calvin turns to a practical question instead: what matters more is that we take flesh as offered by the hand of the Lord, not seizing what appetite desires as robbers do; and he rejects the adage that no one can refresh his body with a morsel of bread without defiling his soul.
4:
What the exception forbids they define alike. Calvin holds that life and blood are put not for different things but for the same, not because blood is the life but because the vital spirits chiefly reside in it; and he dismisses as too trifling the reading that a member cut from a living animal is meant. Gill would rather render it the flesh with its life in its blood, so that a beast designed for food should be properly killed and its blood let out, not devoured alive nor eaten raw. Ellicott takes blood as in apposition to soul, the principle of animation: the blood is its representative, and while man may have the body for food, as the vessel that contains the life, the gift itself must go back to God. Keil applies the rule to living animals and to slaughtered ones not drained.

Whether the prohibition still binds sets Clarke and Calvin flatly against each other on the same text of Acts. Clarke traces it through five stages and insists it was renewed under the Gospel, the Gentile converts being charged to abstain on the authority of the Holy Ghost, and not, as he puts it, for fear of stumbling the converted Jews, which he calls the gloss of theologians; the whole Greek Church, he observes, still obeys it. Calvin holds precisely the gloss Clarke rejects: the restriction was part of the old law, so that Tertullian's report that Christians of his day would not taste the blood of cattle savours of superstition, the apostles having enjoined the rite briefly, not to inject a scruple but to keep a sacred liberty from offending the weak. On the reason they agree better, Calvin and Henry both holding that God meant to accustom men to gentleness, lest those hardened to the blood of beasts should at length not spare human blood.

Wesley meanwhile turns on a fellow commentator by name: Henry has a strange conceit, that the verse is only a prohibition to eat flesh, which does such violence to the text that to mention it is sufficient. At the hand of every beast draws four readings. Ellicott takes it as a command for the extirpation of the carnivora, given at the moment the peaceful animals had been saved. Wesley reads it of executing the particular beast that kills a man, and adds that it would not be unsafe to observe it still. Clarke turns the clause round to face man, as a warning against cruelty to the brute creation, concluding that horse-racers, hare-hunters, bull-baiters and cock-fighters must give account for every creature wantonly destroyed; and he notes that the Samaritan reads living for beast. Calvin makes it an argument from the lesser to the greater: if God is angry with brute creatures hurried by blind impulse to feed upon man, what will become of the man who falls upon his brother.

Whether the sixth verse founds the magistrate's sword three of them say yes. Gill calls it the first law of the kind empowering the magistrate to take life, God having reserved that right before and declined to use it upon Cain; Wesley says the same; Ellicott adds that the penalty is not left to natural law but executed under such safeguards as each country's civil law shall order. Calvin thinks them deceived who suppose a political law is simply intended, since the words are more comprehensive: however magistrates connive, God sends executioners from other quarters, so that some die in highways, some in stews and many in wars. On the reason given, Calvin says God deems himself violated in the person of his image; and Henry and Wesley share one sentence, that such remains of God's image are upon fallen man that he who unjustly kills defaces it and dishonours him.
7:
What kind of covenant this is Gill twice takes pains to deny. It is not the covenant of grace in Christ, he says, but of the preservation of the creatures in common; and when the living creatures are named he repeats it, that this is a further proof it was not the covenant of grace but of conservation, since it is made with irrational as well as rational creatures. Ellicott reads the same fact as an advance: no covenant is mentioned as existing between God and the world before the flood, but here there is a step onward in all respects, man in the renovated earth being brought nearer to God by admission into covenant with him. Henry draws out what the parties imply: God's covenants are made with the covenanters and their seed, and those may be taken in and receive the benefits who cannot restipulate or give their own consent, since this one is made with every living creature. Keil prints the passage without comment.

Calvin traces three steps in it. First God makes the covenant with Noah and his family, lest they should fear a deluge for themselves; secondly he transmits it to posterity, that those afterwards born might apprehend the testimony by faith and conclude that what was promised to the sons of Noah was promised to them; thirdly he declares that he will be propitious to brute animals also, though the effect towards them is the preservation of their lives only, without sense and intelligence. From the second step he turns on his opponents: hence the ignorance of the Anabaptists may be refuted, who deny that the covenant is common to infants because they lack present faith, as if, when God promises salvation to a thousand generations, the fathers were not intermediate parties between God and their children, whose office it is to deliver the promise from hand to hand.

Ellicott alone presses the words for a conclusion about the flood's extent. The covenant reaches, he observes, first to the animals that had been with Noah in the ark and secondly to those that had not, since the verse runs from all that go out of the ark unto every beast of the earth; and takes that phrase to imply a world-sphere beyond Noah's. He then names an opponent: to such straits are those reduced who hold the theory of a universal deluge that Kalisch argues the words mean the fish, as if fishes would be destroyed by a second flood any more than by the first. The assurance, on his reading, is that the animals everywhere shall never again be in danger of a similar extinction.

What the promise does not cover Henry sets out in three limitations: it does not hinder other wasting judgments, for though God has bound himself not to use this arrow again, he has other arrows in his quiver; nor the destruction of particular places by inundation; nor the destruction of the world at the last day by fire. He balances the two worlds, that as the old world was ruined to be a monument of justice, so this remains a monument of mercy; and he and Wesley share a passage almost word for word, that if the sea should flow but for a few days, as it does twice every day for a few hours, what desolation it would make, so that God by flowing seas and sweeping rains shows what he could do in wrath, and by preserving the earth between both what he can do in mercy. Calvin gives the promise a use in the mind: the memory of the deluge might have inspired new terrors whenever the sky was clouded, and that anxiety is taken away; and since impiety overflows now not less than in Noah's age, the waters must be restrained by this word as by a thousand bolts and bars.
12:
Whether there was a rainbow before the flood is the question of the passage, and only Gill leaves it open, Jews and Christians alike being divided. Clarke lays out the optics: the bow is never seen but in showery weather nor unless the sun shines, never but opposite the sun, and always double; since it is the natural effect of the sun's rays refracted in spherical drops, it cannot rationally be supposed there was none before, the Hebrew saying not that the bow is now created but that it has been given. Calvin calls the contrary opinion of certain eminent theologians frivolous: the words do not signify that a bow was then formed which had not existed, but that a mark was engraven upon it. Ellicott dismisses as curious speculation the notion that no rain fell before the flood, and notes with Maimonides that the verb is not I do set but I have set; Wesley says the bow was likely seen before but was never a seal of the covenant till now.

Calvin makes the sign paradoxical: by its own nature the bow might rather signify the contrary, since it threatens continued rain, so that the meaning is: as often as the rain alarms you, look upon the bow, for though it seems to make the rain overflow the earth it is a pledge of returning dryness, and it becomes you to stand with greater confidence than under a serene sky. Henry and Wesley make the same observation in the same words, that the bow appears when the clouds are most disposed to wet, so that when we have most reason to fear the rain God shows this seal that it shall not prevail, and that it appears when one part of the sky is clear, intimating mercy remembered in the midst of wrath, the bow being coloured rain, or the edges of a cloud gilded. Henry adds a step the others do not: the thicker the cloud the brighter the bow, so that as afflictions abound consolations much more abound.

What a sign is Ellicott and Calvin treat differently. Ellicott complains that the word is too often rendered miracle in the New Testament, whereas in most places it is some natural occurrence; and he instances the shepherds' sign, a babe wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger, a thing of the most ordinary kind. He also distinguishes promise from covenant: promises are revocable and may depend on man's co-agency, but a covenant is irrevocable. Calvin takes the occasion for a doctrine of sacraments: signs must never be severed from the word, and a sacrament wrested from the word ceases to be what it is called, since it must be a vocal sign; an administration in which the word is silent is not merely vain but draws with it pure satanic delusions, and by the word he means not that of which the Papists boast, who enchant bread and water and oil with their magical whisperings.

All the classical parallels point one way. Gill notes that the heathen poets call the rainbow the messenger of Juno; Clarke adds that Homer likens the dragons on Agamemnon's breastplate to the rainbow which the son of Saturn placed in the cloud as a sign to mankind, and that Virgil twice has Iris sent from heaven; Ellicott quotes the Chaldean Genesis, where the goddess lifts up the arches which Anu had created as his glory. On what use to make of the sign they part company. Clarke refuses: believing it intended solely for the purpose named in the text, he forbears to make spiritual uses of it, allowing that many have done so edifyingly but denying that such uses have any foundation there. Wesley and Henry make exactly those uses, bidding us look on the bow as God does, that we too may be mindful of the covenant with faith and thankfulness.
18:
The naming of the three sons Henry takes as proof that Noah had no more children after the flood, and draws the moral that God when he pleases can make a little one become a thousand. Calvin puts the same fact to the promise: the enumeration illustrates the force of Replenish the earth, since an immense multitude of men proceeded in a short time from so small a number. Ellicott alone looks forward with foreboding: evil and discord were soon to reappear, though in a milder form, for no brother sheds a brother's blood, but in the next generation sin breaks forth afresh, the descendants of Canaan taking the place of the Cainites, without their striking gifts but foremost as a race in trade and commerce. Keil prints the narrative through to the blessing of Shem without pausing here.

That Noah returned to an old calling rather than took up a new one all four agree. Gill says he was a tiller of the earth as before the flood and now began again, the Jews saying he invented instruments of husbandry and perhaps the plough; Clarke that the phrase means his recommencing operations he had carried on for six hundred years before, interrupted by the flood; Calvin that Noah, with a collected mind and now an old man, returned to his former labours; and Henry that though Noah was a great man and a good man, an old man and a rich man, greatly favoured by heaven, he would not live an idle life nor think the husbandman's calling below him. Clarke pauses over the English word, deriving husband from the Anglo-Saxon for house and a verb meaning to bind, the bond of the house, and citing a fourteenth-century manuscript Bible that writes it house-bond.

Whether Noah is to be blamed sets four of them against each other, and each knows what the others say. Clarke exculpates him entirely: it is very probable this was the first cultivation of the vine and that the intoxicating power of the juice had never been known, so that Noah might have drunk without the least blame. He supports it with a case he says he witnessed, of a man who had drunk only milk or water all his life, was given half a pint of cider in a Somersetshire farmhouse, and within half an hour could neither speak plain nor walk, though of the crime of drunkenness as innocent as an infant. Then he turns on the commentators: some seem glad to fix on such a fact, which by their distortion becomes a crime, and then in a strain of sympathetic tenderness affect to deplore the failings and imperfections of the best of men, when on a proper interpretation neither can appear at all.

Gill offers precisely the formula Clarke scorns: the incident is recorded not to disgrace Noah but to caution men against intemperance, and it shows the best of men are not secure from falling. Calvin rejects the excuse at its root: the opinion that wine was not in use before that time has been the more willingly received as affording an honourable pretext for excusing Noah's sin, but it does not appear probable that the fruit of the vine, which excels all others, should have remained neglected, and Moses does not say Noah was drunken on the first day he tasted it. Leaving the question undetermined, he makes the passage teach what a filthy and detestable crime drunkenness is, since the patriarch, hitherto a rare example of frugality, prostrated himself naked and became a laughingstock, and God has branded him with an eternal mark of disgrace. Wesley sides with Clarke, thinking it highly probable Noah did not know the effect beforehand; Ellicott is severe on another point, that he was uncovered is literally he uncovered himself, no accident but a wilful breach of modesty.
22:
Why the curse falls on Canaan and not Ham divides them sharply. Henry takes the short way, that Canaan is cursed and in him Ham is himself cursed, either as the more guilty son or because his posterity was to be rooted out to make room for Israel. Ellicott denies the transfer. The phrase is literally his son, the little one, which can only mean his youngest; Ham was not the youngest, Japheth was; and it is not Ham who is cursed but Canaan. So far from Ham being accursed, he says, his descendants were building Thebes and Nineveh and Babylon and founding empires while Japheth's wandered over Europe with no better weapons than flint and bone; and for centuries the Egyptians, a Hamite race, made Israel serve them. The application of the curse to Ham, he concludes, seems to have been suggested to commentators by the degradation of the African race in modern times and especially by the prevalence of negro slavery, whereas anciently the converse was the case; we must not extend to Ham the curse pronounced upon Canaan.

If Canaan is meant, what had he done? Ellicott supposes he was himself the offender, the youngest member of the family, and cites a tradition in Origen that Canaan first saw the exposure and told his father, and Aben Ezra's opinion that he had done worse than mock, though Scripture does not reveal the crime; with some such surmise, he says, we must be content. Clarke insists that what is pronounced is prophecy and not temper: on the one the spirit of prophecy, not the incensed father, pronounces a curse, and on the others the same spirit, not parental tenderness, a blessing, so that these things would have occurred as they did had Noah never spoken. Their profligacy, he adds, was not the effect of the curse, but the curse the effect of their foreseen conduct.

Clarke also sets limits. The curse fell neither on Canaan immediately nor on his father but on the Canaanites, and even so does not exclude them from salvation, extending not to the soul and eternity but to their bodies and to time. Ellicott grounds the curse in religion rather than race, since as Shem's blessing is religious so possibly is Canaan's, the people being enslaved by a most degrading idolatry; and he quotes Lenormant, that no other people rivalled them in the mixture of bloodshed and debauchery with which they thought to honour the Deity. Yet he balances it: the race had a great future, the Hittites being among the foremost nations of antiquity and the Sidonians and Tyrians such famous traders that Canaanite is in our version translated merchant. Henry and Wesley, sharing a sentence once more, date the fulfilment to the conquest under Joshua, about eight hundred years after, and add that God often visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children who inherit their dispositions.

On the two brothers Calvin dwells with approval: they turned their eyes from their father's disgrace lest the reverence they owed him be lowered, supposing their own eyes would be polluted if they voluntarily looked; and there is something so unaccountably shameful in the nakedness of man, he adds, that scarcely anyone dares look upon himself even when no witness is present. He then turns the garment against Rome: the Papists make themselves ridiculous in covering the abominations of their whole impure clergy with the cloak of Shem and Japheth, since Antichrist and his horned bishops must first prove themselves fathers if they wish any honour paid them. Wesley says that to have seen it accidentally would have been no crime, but Ham pleased himself with the sight and told his brethren in the street, in a scornful deriding manner; and Gill collects the older charges, that Berosus identified him with Zoroaster, a magician and the public corrupter of mankind.
26:
That Shem's blessing is worded as a doxology all of them notice. Gill says that though the words ascribe blessedness to God, they include the blessing of Shem, and indeed the greatest he could enjoy, since what greater blessing is there than for a man to have God to be his God. Calvin explains the idiom, that the Hebrews, speaking of any transcendent excellence, raise their thoughts to God, so that the holy man, perceiving the grace destined for this son, rises to thanksgiving; whence we infer that he spoke of secret favours deferred to a remote period. Ellicott makes the form the measure of the gift: the greatness of Shem's blessing appears in its taking the form of a hymn of praise, and the patriarch's outburst was a presage of the hallelujahs that were to arise from all mankind for the birth of that son of Shem in whom all nations were to be blessed. Wesley puts it plainly: Shem is recompensed for his respect to his father in this, that the Lord himself puts on him the honour of being his God.

The change of the divine name in the next verse Keil and Ellicott both mark. Keil observes that Noah desired this blessing not from Jehovah, the God of Shem, who bestows saving spiritual good, but from Elohim, God as Creator and Governor, since it respected primarily the blessings of the earth, though Japheth would share the others by dwelling in Shem's tents. Ellicott says the same and presses it into an argument: the names follow one another with extraordinary exactness, so that it is plainly impossible to divide this ancient poem into Elohistic and Jehovistic sections, the theory failing in a crucial place however plausible occasionally. He also recovers a play on the name: the Hebrew is God enlarge the enlarger, not God shall enlarge, the translators having erred as in changing Hebel into Abel.

What dwelling in Shem's tents means they take further apart. Ellicott holds that it is possession and not hospitality: to dwell in the tents of Shem is not so much to share them as to own them, the religious privileges of Shem's race now belonging to Japheth. Wesley offers two readings of the verb. Taking it as enlargement, he sees Japheth's seed made masters of Shem's tents when the Jews were tributaries first to the Grecians and then to the Romans; but the word also signifies to persuade, and read so it speaks the conversion of the Gentiles, so that Jews and Gentiles are united in the gospel fold, and when Japheth joins with Shem, Canaan falls before them both. Keil raises the disputed question of who dwells there, and the block breaks off before the answer.

Of Noah's last years Henry says the long life was a reward of his piety and a blessing to the world, to which he continued a preacher of righteousness, with this advantage, that now all he preached to were his own children; and he closes with an antithesis, that Noah lived to see two worlds, but, being an heir of the righteousness which is by faith, at death went to see a better than either. Calvin balances joy against grief: within a hundred and fifty years his sons' offspring was so numerous as to prove the benediction's efficacy, yet he was compelled to behold the sanctuary of God in Shem's family dilapidated and rent, Abraham's own father having deserted his station and erected a profane tabernacle. Clarke annexes a survey of the three families from Hales: Ham signifies burnt or black, the Hamites being a seafaring race who founded the first great empires; Shem signifies name or renown; Japheth signifies enlargement, his posterity spreading until they encompassed the earth. Ellicott ends on the shortening of life, Noah reaching the antediluvian span while Shem lived six hundred years and Peleg two hundred and thirty-nine.
